incident_description:
Touched oven rack of Anova Precision Oven with one hand while touching oven's built-in food probe with other hand.  Received small but painful electric shock.

Used [REDACTED] digital multimeter with [REDACTED] leads to measure electrical potential between oven rack/oven wall and ground (0V, as required by law and electrical code!) and between food probe and ground.  Food probe was found to be 33V above ground potential.

Unplugged food probe and replaced with identical, factory-original Anova food probe from a different Anova Precision Oven.  Confirmed 33V from food probe tip to known-good electrical ground (conduit entering my kitchen electrical panel), confirmed oven rack and walls were still properly grounded (0V to ground).  Rechecked ground on outlet oven was plugged into vs neutral on same outlet - 0.1V, within normal range.  Rechecked ground against large metallic water pipe - 0V.

Retested over several days after running oven at 500F without steam to determine whether internal condensation or other liquid might be causing an unexpected short.  Retests showed voltage of 31-33V on the probe tip, seemingly varying with input line voltage to the device (which has ranged from 121V to 124V over the past few days due to high electrical demand in our region).  No value lower than 31V was observed between the probe tip and ground.

Conclusion: food probe tip (and presumably food probe connection within its socket) is shorted to a source of about 33V somewhere within the oven.
justification: The incident resulted in a small but painful electric shock, which qualifies as an injury.

incident_description:
I purchased this Ninja Foodi Power Blender & Processor System on 5/28/21 and was injured the second time I used it on 6/2/21 while making a smoothie.  After removing the lid and while pouring, the razor-sharp blade assembly suddenly fell out of the pitcher and struck my right wrist, resulting in a deep cut needing three stitches.  I have a video showing how the blades fall out and razor-sharp the blades are, as well as pictures of my injury.  I was extremely fortunate that the blades did not hit a blood vessel/tendon/ligament and cause more serious injury.  

The design of this blender is absolutely terrible and a hazardous danger to users.  Every other blender IÃÂve used has blades that do not fall out and are part of the pitcher.  With this design, if you are pouring a thicker mixture (like a smoothie), you must reach into the pitcher with your hand to remove the blade assembly, causing a mess to your hand and contaminating the mixture in the process.  Otherwise, the razor-sharp blade assembly will fall out while pouring and cause an injury.  Your other option is to open the tiny spout on the lid, which does not pour out thick contents easily at all.

After getting hurt, I was initially shocked why the manufacturer wouldnÃÂt have warnings to prevent this injury.  The fact that I had to carefully look for such warnings and instructions makes them defective.

The two warnings I could find were on the pitcher lid and the ÃÂQuick StartÃÂ instructions (I have pictures upon request).  

Its lid warning fails to comply with best standard warning practices and ANSI Z535 by failing to mention the specific consequences that result from exposure to the danger. Here, the warning only reads in incredibly small print buried among other instructions, ÃÂCAREFULLY REMOVE STACKED BLADE ASSEMBLY BEFORE POURINGÃÂ.  A proper warning must explain the consequences and use design elements (such as bold print, contrasting colors, borders and underscoring for emphasis, or easily understandable pictures/symbols), for example, ÃÂBLADE ASSEMBLY WILL FALL OUT IF POURING WHILE LID IS REMOVED.ÃÂ  Not mentioning the consequences and hiding the instruction in a sea of small print is like saying, ÃÂDo not eat thisÃÂ in tiny letters ÃÂ it fails to explain what will happen if you DO eat the item.

The ÃÂQuick StartÃÂ instructions are equally defective by putting its warning (which ÃÂ unlike the lid warning ÃÂ correctly states what the consequence is of failing to remove the blades while pouring without a lid) at the bottom of the page in even smaller print (see picture), FAR away from the main instructions for the blender.  The manufacturer should have used ANSI-required ÃÂembeddedÃÂ warnings that are placed closely to the applicable instruction so that users immediately understand the danger associated with a particular step.  

Here, the instruction should have read (new language in ALL CAPS):

. . .  2.  Fill pitcher with desired ingredients.  Install the lid, then lower lid handle to lock in place.  WARNING:  LOCKING THE LID IN PLACE ALSO LOCKS THE BLADES IN PLACE.  UNLOCKING AND REMOVING THE LID ALSO UNLOCKS THE BLADES, WHICH MAY FALL OUT IF THE PITCHER IS TILTED TO POUR OUT A MIXTURE.

Even if an owner of the blender is fortunate enough to find, read and understand either the lid warning or the ÃÂQuick StartÃÂ instructions, the reality is that other casual users (such as guests or other family members) likely will neither see the incredibly small-printed defective warning on the lid or have the ÃÂQuick StartÃÂ instructions available to them.  The blender is therefore a hazard to both the party guest who makes a thick, slushy-type margarita, and takes off the lid to pour it out, and the visiting family member casually doing the dishes and washing the blender ÃÂ both may be seriously injured by falling blades pouring out that margarita or water used to rinse the pitcher without the lid attached and blades removed.

THE MANUFACTURER HAS FAILED IN ITS DUTY TO REPORT THIS INCIDENT, NECESSITATING ME TO DO IT.

Report Update - 7/28/21

The defectiveness of the warnings and design accompanying the Ninja Foodi blender on which I was injured is established by the warnings that I believe were approved by the CPSC in connection with the Ninja BL660 series blender recall, which design is identical in terms of the removable stacked blade design.  

In short, despite knowing precisely what warning would be sufficient to users of the Foodi blender by way of the BL660 series recall, SharkNinja proceeded to use different and defective warnings.  

Attached are the warnings accompanying both the BL660 and the Foodi, and they are strikingly different, with the BL660 warning addressing several of the concerns noted in my report to the CPSC, including:
ÃÂ	ANSI Embedded Warnings:  The BL660 warning has the warning language right after the appropriate instruction, whereas the Foodi warning has the warning language at the bottom of the page in smaller font away from the relevant instruction.
ÃÂ	Pictograms:  The BL660 warning has pictograms showing exactly what should be done, whereas the Foodi warning does not.
ÃÂ	Separate Pamphlet:  The BL660 blade warning was a separate pamphlet, calling more attention to the danger.  The Foodi warning again is all but buried and hidden at the bottom of a "QuickStart" pamphlet. If I had received a separate pamphlet, I more likely would have seen the warning and appreciated the risk.
Based on the above drastic differences in warnings, I strongly believe the CPSC should find Ninja's Foodi blender current warnings defective and deficient and order a new recall mandating inclusion of the "Stacked Blade Assembly" warnings that accompanied the BL660 series blenders.  The current warning on the Foodi blender is not embedded, located at the bottom of the page in smaller font, contains no pictograms, and does not adequately instruct users of the dangers of the defective stacked blade assembly design.
justification: The incident resulted in a deep cut requiring stitches, indicating an injury (severity 3). The design flaw and inadequate warnings make such injuries likely (likelihood 4).

incident_description:
Oster Blender | Pro 1200 with Glass Jar, 24-Ounce Smoothie Cup and Food Processor Attachment, Brushed Nickel purchased from Amazon in August of 2016.  (Amazon lists it as BLSTMB-CBF-000).  10 months after purchase, the blades snapped off in my shake --which I did not know until I took a tablespoonful of my shake.  I alerted Oster and Amazon about this.  Oster removed my product review and sent a brand new replacement blender ÃÂ the exact same model.  I assumed that because they sent the exact same model blender that meant the issue was an anomaly and not a design or material flaw.  

In 2021 3 ÃÂ½ years after I received the replacement Oster Pro 1200 Blender, the blade broke in half in my smoothie and I did not know until I spooned the two pieces into my mouth.  Before having my smoothie, I even make a point of just checking the blade/housing.  It looked ÃÂfineÃÂ - the blades are layered so I couldnÃÂt tell by sight that anything broke-until I found the blades in my mouth, again.  I have made smoothies every day for 3 decades using the single purpose, no frills Oster Blenders at work.  After thousands of days of daily use with plain Oster blender --- no blade ever broke.  This is a design flaw.

Another user, a mother of a 3-year-old shared same photos of broken blades coming off in the food she was about to serve her 3 year old son.  This is a hazardous design flaw.  Yet Oster continues to sell the blender on third party sites, like Amazon and [REDACTED].  I checked. They just restocked inventory on Amazon ~June 23, 2021 well after I notified them and flagged prior occurrences for me and for another user.

Oster has warning about sharp blades in their materials.  I am lucky I didn't cut my mouth either time.  Or start to swallow.  Oster knows about each incident.  I contacted them repeatedly to say this is a dangerous product.  I really  hope they  have their newer combo Blender/Food Processor evaluated in a lab to make sure the blades or the drive will not cause this to happen again to someone.

incident_description:

I called Frigidaire customer service first thing this morning and was told that there werenÃÂt any previous complaints on this type of occurrence nor were there any recalls so the best she could do was give me a discount on the replacement glass and send a tech out to install it at my expense. I asked to speak to a manager at this point and was eventually sent to a problem resolution specialist who basically told me the same thing. It was obvious they were following a script, and were only there to deflect any sort of complaint and simply offer the bare minimum. In fact when I told them that it was lucky that no one had their face near the glass and that there would have been a totally different conversation of myself or one of my family members such as my granddaughter had the glass explode in their face resulting in permanent injury the problem resolution person agrees that then the liability department would have handled it and since this was a hypothetical situation (even though I had just had my face in front of the glass no more than three minutes prior to the explosion of glass) there was nothing else they could offer. I told her that it was unreasonable and poor service on the part of Frigidaire to not offer at minimum the replacement part and installation for free due to the circumstances. This situation is not like an electrical issue, or an element going out. This was obviously a flaw in the glass that finally gave out. She said flaws would show up in one to two years of service. I said that might be for someone who used their oven much more than we do. I am absolutely disappointed, not in the ladies I spoke to as they are only doing their job, but in the overall response to this situation. I have purchased Frigidaire appliances in the past and will no longer purchase any nor will I recommend them. I asked the last lady in problem resolution for her manager and she said they werenÃÂt available and would call me in one or two business days. This is also totally unacceptable. I am beyond disappointed and frustrated. Something that could have been resolved easily by sending glass free of charge and installing free of charge that would have made for a happy lifetime customer who would spread the word to other potential customers instead created a frustrated, unhappy customer who will never buy another Frigidaire or Electrolux product.

When he tried to stop the roaster, none of the buttons he pressed, stopped the machine.  The consumer grabbed a glove and removed the drum.

12/2020:  The consumer contacted the firm and reported the issue to the firm.  He received an email back from the firm indicating that they would review the matter and investigate it further.  It was also suggested that he re-bend the ÃÂyokeÃÂ, which he did.  He has not experienced that problem again.


4/2021:  The roaster has 2 modes.  One is automatic and the other is manual.  He had always used manual, but he recently used the machine in the program mode.  The P5- setting is the hottest in the manual mode and the P1- setting, is the hottest for automatic.  ItÃÂs unclear why they are reversed, depending on the mode.   Part of the way through the roasting process, he changed the setting.  The roaster started the second crack, the consumer pressed the cooling option and the fan rotation changed.  He walked away thinking it was cooling.

The consumer stopped the machine (unsure how).  He did not notice any damage to the machine, but was concerned that the coffee beans might catch fire. incident_description:
My Samsung refrigerator has had ice building up behind the back panel, which impacts the fan movement. Additionally, it interferes  with  the temperature sensor &, despite the refrigerator itself indicating otherwise, temperatures increased to about 47 degrees, which is hazardous for food safety. 
This is a known defect with all Samsung French door Refrigerators, as indicated on their service bulletins, but it is not well known to consumers.
justification: The incident involves a known defect causing food safety hazards but no reported injury or death.

incident_description: My wife and I bought a Samsung refrigerator about 6 years ago, on May 16th 2021 I became very ill to the point of passing out and extreme weakness. I was hospitalized and diagnosed with food poising. The medical staff tried to track down the source by having me recall the food I had eaten over the past 24 hours. I recovered at home on May 17th and was not able to eat anything until the evening of May 18th. It was then it was discovered that our refrigerator felt warm inside. We placed an outdoor wireless thermometer in the  refrigerator and found it was running at a temp of 55 degrees F, even though the fridge display showed the unit was set to 38 degrees.  After some research I found the issue with the fridge, it had iced up and had caused stress fractures beside the cooling unit. I managed to get it working again by defrosting the ice build up but after 10 days it went down again, luckily I never removed the thermometer and was able to see the temp rising. Again I removed the inside back panel and it was iced up yet again, this time the ice filled the fan and I had to order a replacement fan. Early this morning it happened for the 3rd time, same temp rise and massive ice build up. At 1:00am I had to disassemble the fridge again before I lost yet another fridge full of food.
justification: The incident resulted in injury (food poisoning requiring hospitalization), but the likelihood of recurrence is unlikely as it depends on specific refrigerator malfunctions.

incident_description:

The consumer said if young children or pets were near the door, it could present a substantial safety issue.

incident_description: Our new LG electric range is entirely too easy to turn the burner on.  We've had 2 fires on the stove top when the stove was not being used.  The first time was about a month ago and a pizza box that was placed on the stove ignited.  There was nothing cooking on the stovetop.  We got our pizza and went to the living room and smoke filtering in alerted us to the fire.  I thought it was a fluke accident.  The second time, my son was heating chili in the microwave above the stove.  He set the microwave cover on the stove stove to get his chili out and went to the living room.  Again, smoke filtering in to the living room alerted us to a fire (melting).  Both times, the knob was on high when we looked at the stove.  After that happened, I knew it wasn't a fluke, but a real safety hazard.  Thinking back, there were times I was cooking and I noticed the warming burner was on and I had not turned it on.  The knobs have been "turned on" by everyone in the family so it's not just a coincidence that someone is just the right height or moves past the knobs just the right way.  The range was not being used in any way during the 2 fires.  Luckily there were no injuries and we were in the next room when the smoke billowed in.
justification: The incident describes fires caused by the stove being turned on unintentionally, but no injuries or deaths occurred.

incident_description:
My husband and I purchased the Samsung French Door refrigerator, model number RF428HARS, April 1, 2013 for $2,390.37. We thought we were buying a top-of-the-line unit. Little did we know this refrigerator had design defects which cause the ice maker to freeze up and not work, water leakage under the drawers and out onto the floor, and loud fan noise that stops when the doors are opened. According to Samsung's Service Bulletin #A5C20140703001 dated 10/13/2015, this is caused by a defect in manufacturing which causes ice to form at the top of the evaporator and interfere with the fans operation. We have had to unplug the refrigerator for 24 hours to defrost the refrigerator and freezer many, many times which is a huge mess of water everywhere and the loss of food. The refrigerator also does not maintain a safe temperature level reaching 50 degress in some areas when set to 38 degrees on the control panel causing unsafe food and food loss. I am a member of a [REDACTED] group with more 56,000 members (and growing daily) who all have the same issues with this defective French Door Samsung design. There are 20 models in a class action lawsuit all with these same issues and there are no fixes. Samsung has been aware of this design defect for years but they are still selling them and give people the run around about refunds. Please check out the [REDACTED] group Samsung Refrigerator Recall U.S.A. Now
This unit is out of warranty, but being as it was a defective design and cannot be fixed, I would like to be remibursed. We bought this refrigerator in good faith that the quality was as advertised but we have been very disappointed. People need to know about these high-priced defective and dangerous refrigerators. 

Thank you, please help make this right.
justification: The refrigerator's failure to maintain safe temperatures and the resulting food spoilage pose a health risk, but there is no mention of actual injury or death.

incident_description:
Five months ago my sister and I purchased a GE Self-Cleaning Range.  On Sunday, She placed it into the self-cleaning mode.  At first there was a warning beep and an indicator that the door needed to be locked.  Once that was done, it went into the self-cleaning mode.  
Within the first hour, smoke detectors began to beep (which we expected).  Within the first hour and a half, I noticed that the door was open approximately 2 inches.  I asked my sister if she had opened the door and she told me she had not.  Upon closer inspection we found the oven still in the cleaning mode and VERY hot, the latch handle completely melted into two.  We turned the oven off.  

Our concern is that the oven should have never continued in self-cleaning mode once the door was opened.    A certified repair man informed us that he has been called out for numerous repairs similar to ours.  This malfunction is a failure of a safety feature that puts consumers at risk.  If we had small children, they could have been severely burned with the excessive heat.  We could have had a fire.  The latch handle provides no guarantee that the door will not open when it is burned off.
justification: The incident involved a safety feature failure that could have led to injury or fire, but no actual injury occurred. The repairman's report suggests this malfunction is not rare.

[REDACTED]

incident_description:
Here is a copy of the information that I sent to the manufacturer:
I own a Jenn-Air cooktop (propane gas). Model number - JGD3536BS00; Serial number - D63208434. I purchased it new on Jan 5, 2018 (receipt attached).On Jan 14, 2021, one of the cooktop's burner valves locked in the OFF position. It was not possible to move the valve at all. Replacement was necessary; the repair cost was $238.19, about 15% of the price of the new cooktop - receipt attached. It was annoying to experience such a serious failure in a virtually new cooktop. But we were able to use the cooktop with one inoperable burner until the repair was completed.Today, we experienced another similar failure. However, this failure raises SERIOUS SAFETY concerns. My wife was cooking and called me for assistance when she was unable to adjust the flame or turn off a burner (NOT the one that was just replaced). Another burner valve was locked but this time, it was locked in the ON position. There was no indication of aÃÂ problem when my wife turned the burner on.I removed theÃÂ pan from the flaming burner and attempted to move the valve so that it could be turned off. After some effort, I was able to get the valve to the off position. The flame went out so I assume the gas flow fully stopped. TheÃÂ valve is currently immovable. I continually check theÃÂ affected burner toÃÂ ensure there is no gas leakage from theÃÂ broken valve. One obvious safety concern is the reality that most people do not know how to turn off gas to their cooktop,ÃÂ including my wife. If the flame went out, propane would have been released into the house, creating an emergency.I owned a Jenn-Air cooktop for 20 years before buying this new unit as its replacement. There were no problems whatsoever with the original unit over its lifetime. Consequently, I bought another Jenn-Air. By any measure, there is a fundamental safety defect in the valve units of this new model. I'm a retired guy who has had many gas stoves throughout my life. NEVER have I experienced this type of failure. Experiencing TWO serious failures within less than four months is sufficient for me to conclude that this potential hazard must be remedied ASAP or this cooktop will have to be discarded. A copy of this email is being sent to the Consumer Product Safety Commission.
justification: The incident involved a gas cooktop valve failure that could have led to a gas leak, posing a serious safety risk, though no injury or death occurred.

incident_description:
When did this happen?

-- March 19, 2021 at approximately 6pm PDT.

What happened that made you want to report?

-- I had a roast cooking in the oven. I had to run an errand. When I returned home and unlocking and opening my apartment door, I instantly smelled gas. Not strong, yet definitely noticeable and more so towards the kitchen. I left the front door open. I then went directly to the gas stove. I verified that, even though the electronic display indicated that the oven temperature was still set to 350 degrees, there was virtually no heat emanating from the oven's vent on the top of the stove. I pressed the oven's Clear/Off button. I then opened several windows throughout my apartment, starting with the kitchen window, in order to ventilate my apartment. It was a somewhat breezy day and it didn't take long for the smell of gas to go away. I then went back to the oven. I unplugged it's power cord for 60 seconds. I then plugged the power cord back in.

A potentially related incident occured the day before. My apartment building is undergoing reovations in order to make the building more resistant to earthquakes. The construction people tripped the power breaker for the outlets in the laundry room. They had no idea which breaker they tripped, so they flipped all breakers at least twice and within 5 seconds for each breaker for all units within the apartment building. I was home when this occurred. I had to reset the clocks on my oven and on my microwave. One of the construction workers knocked on my door. I had to show him which circuit breakers were separately for the building itself, and not for any of the apartment units. I then had to point out the specific tripped breaker for the laundry room, and explain that in order to reset it, you have to flip it entirely off and then flip it back on.

I specifically mention the above paragraph since I hypothesise that the oven's electronics, due to the two rapid on-off flips of my apartment's circuit breaker, may have scrambled the oven's electronics. I specifically ask that the CPSC follow up with the consumer who reported their incident which is related to the following recall number 12-737:

https://www.cpsc.gov/Recalls/2012/frigidaire-gas-range-recalled-due-to-fire-hazard-sold-exclusively-at-lowes-stores

if the consumer related to recall number 12-737 also recalls any power glitches shortly prior to his or her incident, such that this consumer recalls having to reset the oven's clock time.

What type of product(s) were being used?

-- Frigidaire gas oven, model number FFGF3011LWF, Serial No. VF54325718

Who was using the product(s)?

-- Myself.

How were the product(s) being used?

-- Cooking.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?

-- No.

How did any injuries occur?

-- No injuries / Not applicable.

Here is an update for my report:
I subsequently suspected that the igniter for the oven was going bad since the oven would no
longer heat up. I removed the igniter and measured its resistance. The resistance was 377
Ohms. The igniter's part number is 316489408.
I replaced the igniter with the current OEM replacement igniter for the old igniter part number.
The new igniter's part number is 5304509706. I measured teh resistance of the new igniter
before installing it. The resistance of the new igniter is 108 Ohms. Clearly the old igniter was
bad, yet enough current flowed through it to the bimetal valve which allowed gas to flow into
the burner. The igniter was not hot enough to ignite the gas. This is why I smelled gas when I
entered my home after returning from an errand.
Frigidaire and other gas oven manufacturers should be required to add a current detection
circuit for the igniter which would prevent the igniter from remaining on if the detected current
is too low in order to allow the igniter to become hot enough to ignite the gas, yet there might
be enough current flowing through the igniter to improperly allow the bimetal gas valve to
open. An alternative circuit would be for the oven to measure the resistance of the igniter
circuit when the oven not in use and when the oven has cooled off to less than 120 degrees. If
the resistance is higher than 250 Ohms, the oven should display a service code on its
temperature display. IF the resistance is higher than 300 Ohms, then the oven should lock out
all use of the oven.
Obviously measured current and resistance values will vary depending on the make and model
of gas oven. The above is merely an example for what I think would be appropriate for my
Frigidaire gas oven or other gas ovens which use this igniter or very similar igniters.
justification: The incident involved a gas leak due to a faulty igniter, but no injuries or deaths occurred.

incident_description: In January my Wife and I purchased a brand new Over-the-hood Microwave from Spencers TV and Appliances.  This was to replace a 26yr old [REDACTED] that was not matching the current appliance scheme.  The [REDACTED] never, ever had any problems and worked until the day that I deinstalled it.  The new Kitchen Aid unit has all the newest features including a step by step cooking system.  My daughters have been in remote learning and I wanted a unit that would have step by step auto cooking features for them at lunch breaks.  On Tuesday March 30th my daughter put water and rice into a microwave bowl following the step by step instructions.  The unit has an automated sensor system that stops cooking when it is done.  Both my daughters had cooked rice in this many times with no issues.  In this instance the Microwave did not stop cooking, my Wife working from home smelled smoke and went in to the kitchen to find out what happened.   My daughter [REDACTED] said it did not stop cooking and burned down the rice into a crisp and even melted the plastic inside the microwave.  This type of melted plastic has fully contaminated the unit and can not be removed without taking the unit fully apart.  The unit is still under the 1 year warranty so I contacted Kitchen Aid (Whirlpool) about the incident.  The technician from Guinco just left.  He made a full report to the Whirlpool safety department.  When I called them they said there was nothing further they could do since I would not accept anything but a replacement.  They said there only responsibility is to repair it.  It doesnÃÂt matter that everything being cooked in this unit going forward will contaminate all the food cooked in it.  They are not responsible for the safety issue that their unit failed to stop cooking even after it had melted the plastic turntable gear.  They are only responsible for repair of a unit that not only poses a huge fire risk but because it did not function in a safe way is forever contaminated with the chemical residue of the turntable gear plastic.  I will not operate/use a product that would not only destroy the taste of all food but potentially contaminate the food with Petroleum Byproducts.  A 2 month old microwave should never ever get so hot it melts the plastic microwave parts.

incident_description: My wife set the thermostat on the lower oven of the GE Monogram double wall ovens to "Convection Bake" and 350 degrees.  A couple of minutes later she called me in because of a large amount of smoke and a strong burning smell coming from the oven.  We shut the ovens off and the smoke quickly disappeared.  The next day we turned the unit on to see if the problem was the oven or if there was some burnt food inside.  About 2 minutes into pre-heating, loud pops, sparks, and flames started flashing in the space between the two ovens. I quickly shut down the oven and the sparks flashed a few more times before finally stopping.  I shined a flashlight into the space to make sure the flames were out and could see a burnt electrical board with components that appeared melted and badly charged connectors.

incident_description: We bought a home last month that was built in 2015.  All appliances are from LG.  The LG range stove top knobs (Model No. LDE4413ST, Serial No. 511KMEM01140)  are easily bumped and activated into full (HI) operation by bumping the knob "Clockwise".  30 minutes ago I put a reusable plastic grocery tote bag onto the largest electric burner and accidentally "bumped" the knob responsible for that burner.  In no time, the bag melted generating an incredible amount of smoke which, thankfully, caught my attention.  The knobs on this LG stove should be much, much harder to turn in either direction (Right - HI, Left - LOW).    I feel this is an accident ready to happen and I'm concerned that an adult (or child) could be easily burned, or worse, the house may be at risk of "going up in flames".  Too scary that this happened so quickly and thank goodness, I was there to return the knob to the "Off" position, extinguish the "smelting" plastic bag and ventilate our home.
justification: The incident involved a melted plastic bag and smoke but no injury, indicating a severity level of 2. The likelihood is high (4) due to the easily bumped knobs and potential for frequent accidents.

incident_description:
The consumer had the oven mitts sitting on top of the stove for 5 minutes.  None of the burners were on, but the oven was on.  The oven was set to 350 degrees and had been on for approximately 15 minutes.  The consumer slid her hand into the grove.  Immediately, the glove on her right hand began melting around her right hand.  She quickly used her left hand to remove the glove, but pieces of the melted glove were stuck to both of her hands.

She immediately, placed her hands under cold water and caller for her son's assistance.

The consumer had her private nurse come to her home.  The nurse inspected her hands and advised her to place them into ice water.  She then applied burn cream and bandages to the consumer's hands.  She sustained 2nd & 3rd degree burns to both hands

Next, the consumer consulted various attorneys and contacted the firm afterwards.

2/2021:  The consumer wrote a review in the retailers web site, about her experience with the product.  She has not heard back from the firm.

The consumer used the gloves in the past without any incident.  The consumer has wiped the gloves off with a wet sponge, but has never needed to wash them.
justification: The consumer sustained 2nd & 3rd degree burns to both hands, indicating an injury (severity 3). The incident occurred despite prior use without issues, suggesting it's unlikely (likelihood 2).

incident_description: I have a Samsung refridgerator model RF25HMEDBSR/AA with a manufacture date of 10/2015, which conveyed with my home purchase in 2019.  We have had problems with the ice maker and a few weeks ago started to hear loud noises like water trickling and loud motor sounds (like a jet engine taking off).  I noticed water under the crisper drawers.  Then I noticed that the food in the refrigerator did not feel as cold as it has before.  I put a thermometer in the fridge and discovered it was 53 degrees.  It is set at 38, and the digital display read 38.  Anything above 40 degrees is not food safe.  I did some internet research and found that this is a known defect with a Samsung service bulletin number ASC201407030001 dated 10/13/2015 acknowledging the issue that causes all the symptoms my fridge was having.  I called Samsung, and was refused a repair on a defect they know about.  I used the force defrost  setting on the fridge based on guidence I found online and enough ice melted on the sensor that displays the temperature in the fridge to tell me that it was above 50 degrees all the time.  A few days it was up to 60 degrees. I have a small child and cannot risk food poisoning because my refrigerator is unreliable in keeping food cold, its sole purpose!
justification: The refrigerator's failure to maintain safe temperatures poses a risk of foodborne illness (injury), and the issue is a known defect with documented occurrences.

incident_description: I own a Whirlpool Refrigerator/Freezer with ice and water in the door.   The dispenser motor had stopped working several months ago.  After replacing the motor and the control board, it still didn't work.  Then suddenly I saw sparks ark out of the bottom of the door.  I thought it was from the motor since it looked like ice had jammed the agitator.   After that arc, the ice maker stopped producing ice completely.  I did some more troubleshooting today after reading some hints on the web and one said to check the wiring loom that comes out of the bottom of the door.  Sure enough, due to a terrible design flaw, the entire wiring harness had been severed.  That explains the arcing and sparks coming out of the bottom of the door.  This item should be recalled due to safety issues as it prevents serious danger to consumers.

My fridge should do what itÃÂ is designed to do, keep my food cold, keep my food from spoiling, and keep my food at a healthy temperature!ÃÂ  It does none of this!! It doesn't even make ice! incident_description: I was using a Cuisinart vegetable and fruit chopper to dice an onion in the manner directed by the included instructions and later found several small pieces of plastic in the bag that I used to store the chopped onion. Upon close inspection of the chopper, there were several irregularities in the plastic teeth that push the food through the slicing blade. It appears as though the plastic pegs that push the food through the slicing blade plate aren't aligned properly, resulting in the blade plate slicing off bits of plastic, which end up in the food. The pieces of plastic that I found varied in size from 1 or 2 mm up to 12 mm. incident_description: On Friday afternoon, March 19th, 2021, I was using the self-clean option on my IKEA Nutid (Whirlpool) 2016 convection oven on the shortest cycle available (3 hours) when I heard a loud explosion less than one hour into the cycle, presumably as soon as the oven reached temperature. The inner tempered glass door had shattered shooting hot glass all over the inside of the oven and across the floor in front of the oven. I am still finding shards of glass in distant places in my kitchen, and it continues to present a sharps hazard. The oven was less than 5 years old and was not often used and was not very dirty. In fact, the self-clean option had never been used before, although I have used self-clean options many times on other ovens. I had removed the grates from the inside of the oven and followed the instructions for the self-clean operation. The oven was not visibly damaged in any way prior to the incident. Luckily, no one was near the oven, but 500-degree Fahrenheit glass that shot out from the oven could have easily significantly injured anyone walking near the oven at the time of the incident, especially if it had been a pet or a child or if someone had been at eye level with the oven, bending down to grab a pan from a nearby cabinet or to sweep up dust from the floor. Additionally, my family has to wear shoes at all times, as we are still finding shards of glass despite having swept many times.
justification: The incident involved a dangerous explosion of hot glass, but no one was injured. Such events are unlikely given proper oven use and maintenance.

incident_description: I purchased a Samsung refrigerator in December of 2015.  About 2 years ago, we started having issues with the in-door ice maker.  It freezes up and stops producing ice.  Water drips from the ice maker down the fridge.  We need to defrost the ice maker bi-weekly or the ice buildup causes the fan to stop. incident_description:

We have turned the oven on since thanskgiving and the flames keep shooting out of this ven (my husband has video and pictures I can send to reflect this). incident_description:
The consumer indicates that his Thermadore oven has a selection for bake and broil. When owner selects broil, in a two selection process. It takes approximately (5) minutes for the broiler to ignite once propane is introduced. Normal ignition time should be 2-3 minutes. Because of this a propane bubble is built up. When broiler finally ignites there is frequently an explosion inside the oven. Sometimes the explosion is strong enough to 'blow' the oven door down. Consumer notes that if ignitor was not weak no explosion would occur.

1/20/21 -A representative from Thermadore came to consumers home to inspect the oven range and broiler problem. The inspector looked inside the oven and never took any broiler harnesses off to look
at ignitor. The representative informed the consumer that the ignitor was again weak after a past 2&3/4 year replacement. He informed consumer that ignitors should be replaced every three years. The inspector stated that he really did not have to look closer at the problem as this is a frequent happening. That consumer was going on (3) years of use thus needing a new ignitor replacement. Consumer would have to pay out of pocket for any repairs.

Past inspectors, not this one, stated to consumer that he cooked too close to broiler flame. Just an excuse. Consumer notes that the oven racks are factory immoveable. (ie: made to be stationary)

1/21/2020: Consumer set oven to broil and an explosion occurred that was strong enough to lift the stove off the floor for a second.

Consumer noted that the oven explosion happens about 90% of the time when broiler selection is initiated. At times the explosion is small and not forceful. Reason is that the ignition sequence is less  than 5 min. Less propane build up. Consumer further states that the explosion only occurs when oven is set to broil, not in the bake mode. Consumer states that the explosions have gotten progressively worse since last new ignition installation 2&3/4 years ago.

After the broil explosions oven works as it should in broiling said food.

Consumer states that the (4) burner cook top is used about three times daily. Whereas the broiler section of the stove is used about three to four times a Week.

Major point: Consumer/ owner of range certifies that the broiler Igniter on this model has been replaced three times before. The oven igniter ,once before, as he recollects.(original oven range Model Number was PR0304EH106.

Enclosed are all past receipts as evidence of past ignitor failures. The range was completely changed about eleven years ago. Written evidence is enclosed.

The consumer plans on keeping this cooking stove described at least for the next 60 days incase an investigation ensues. Consumer urges a recall of total ignition design.
justification: The incident involves explosions strong enough to lift the stove off the floor, posing a significant risk of injury, though no injury is reported.

incident_description:
Background

I have used Duralex glassware for years.  In 2019-2020 when I moved into a new house, I added some larger sized glasses. I purchased 12.5 oz and 17oz tumblers from Crate & Barrel.   I am a single, so the glasses do not get much use and they are all less than 2 years old, some just a year old. 


Incident

17-Feb-2021, while unloading the dishwasher at around 1pm, one of the 12.5 oz tumblers exploded as I touched it to remove it from the dishwasher.  The dishwasher is a top-load drawer-type dishwasher.  The force was enough to blow glass up (20 inches) from the dishwasher and send it onto the counter and floor 4-5 feet on either side of the dishwasher.  There were 3 types of broken glass: squarish pieces 1-2cm in diameter, small shards, and a fine glass dust.  

Fortunately, I got none of the larger pieces in my eyes, but I did get some of the glass dust in my eyes.  

I called my ophthalmologist.  The office advised me to flush my eyes and apply artificial tears today and to call them back the next day if the irritation persists.   The irrigation is persistent and my right eye and I will go in for a checkup.  It feels like I have some sand in my right eye.  

I did a [REDACTED] search on "duralex exploding" and there is an [REDACTED] discussion of the topic as well as others sharing their experiences.  I was shocked.  I had no idea.  I would not purchase a product that had the potential to explode upon touch.  The product is said to be dishwasher safe, so there was no reason for it to explode as I unloaded the dishwasher. 

I called Duralex.  They said they could send me some information on exploding glass.  The customer service agent volunteered she had Duralex Picardie glassware explode in her cupboard once.  Other than that, I got stalling and a repeated offer to send me info on their glass.

I asked to talk to a manager, because this is a serious safety issue.  I got voicemail of someone of a [REDACTED]  I left a message but did not heard back.

Duralex offered to replace the piece.  I said I was not interested in a replacement.  I no longer wish to used my Duralex.  In my view, it is clearly unsafe.  

What troubles me and the reason for my complaint is that this is a known problem with Duralex glass.  Duralex told me this is a problem in older glassware.  They said glass is made of layers and it can break down over time.   Nonsense!  My glassware was no more than 2 or 2-1/2 years old, lightly used and well-taken care of.  

I notified Crate & Barrel, where I purchased the glassware.  Unlike Duralex, they were concerned and followed up immediately.  They offered me a full refund.  I said I want them to do more than that.  I want them to do their own investigation of the glassware and the potential for explosion and after that if they continue to sell it to provide some kind of warning to consumers.

With regard to the product itself, I regard it as unsafe.  I have sustained an injury that I will need treated.  It could have been MUCH more serious.
justification: The incident resulted in eye irritation requiring medical attention, classifying it as an injury (severity level 3). The occurrence likelihood is rated as 3 (possible) based on the description of similar incidents found online and the customer service agent's personal experience.

I yanked the plug from the wall to avoid a fire.   I have no doubt that the appliance would have caught on fire if it had been left to toast as usual. incident_description: Our Ninja Coffee Bar coffee maker caught fire.  Normally my husband is gone at that time, but luckily for us he was home and in the kitchen when it started to spark and arc and smoke and he immediately took it outside.  Had he not been home, it would have progressed and we could have had a kitchen or house fire, since I was in the other part of the house taking a shower! We could have been injured or worse! The coffee maker had brewed a pot of coffee an hour before and it was just keeping warm.  The unit was two years old. My daughter and son-in-law have the same unit as do his parents.  Will it happen to them? Ninja has been uncaring and will not return my phone calls.  I even offered to ship the unit back to them so they can figure this out.  The people who answer their customer service line gave me a case number and told me someone would call me back.  Two days later I called them and had to repeat my story to customer service and I was told someone would contact me in 3-5 days.  This unit cost over $200 and the only thing customer service says is that it's out of warranty.  Is it OK for a company to feel they have no responsibility for the safety of consumers after two years? That I should expect that a fire could occur and be OK with that?
justification: The coffee maker caught fire but was promptly handled without injury, indicating an incident with no harm. The likelihood is unlikely as it's a specific malfunction in a two-year-old unit.

incident_description: I had a three-quart glass pyrex dish that I attempted to use to roast tomatoes and feta this evening. The glass dish was room temperature as were the tomatoes. The feta was chilled. I placed the rectangle of feta in the middle of the dish with the cherry tomatoes surrounding it. A few drizzles of olive oil and seasonings and I put it in a 400-degree oven for 30 minutes. After 17 minutes, I heard what sounded like a small bomb in the oven. I was in disbelief that the sound came from my oven, but I could hear sizzling so I turned off the oven. I opened it up and the entire dish had shattered into hundreds of pieces. It literally exploded. I was very lucky that this didn't happen while I was holding the dish as I could have been injured. I thought the whole point of Pyrex dishes was to use them for baking? This was at a hot but not extremely hot temperature and there was no sudden change from hot to cold or vice versa. I have several other pyrex dishes and storage containers and now I am very nervous about continuing their use. I hated wasting the ingredients from the meal I was attempting to prepare, but obviously, I had to throw everything away and thoroughly clean my oven. Some of the glass and food even ended up in the vents where the gas-fueled flames heat the oven. I really, really hope that my oven does not malfunction after this.
justification: The glass dish shattered but no one was injured, making it an incident with no injury. Pyrex explosions are rare under normal use conditions.

incident_description:
I purchased my Samsung refrigerator Model RF28HMEDBSR/AA in April 2017 from HHGregg.
 Since I purchased the fridge, I have had nothing but problems with it non-stop. Here are the issues currently affecting my appliance:

1. Ice maker is constantly frozen over and jammed up. If I defrost the fridge for hours (putting my food at risk of spoiling), it's fixed for a couple of days and starts all over again. This is a known product defect and is not a warranty issue.

2. This month, a terrible chemical smell has started building up inside of the appliance. My food started smelling like the chemical that has been leaking in, and is now beginning to taste like it too. I have 2 small children, and I do not feel comfortable feeding them food from a fridge that makes it taste like a potentially poisonous chemical. Who knows what kind of harm could come from me feeding my family food from this fridge.

3. The flex zone drawer is broken. A few years ago, the button would go haywire and start pressing itself, beeping constantly for hours, even through the night, changing modes. Now, the button has completely broken and is stuck at 29 degrees, freezing the contents of my drawer.

4. Temperature is not consistent throughout the appliance. Food in the back of my fridge freezes, while food in the front is okay. Food in the top pull out drawer of my freezer is constantly covered in ice because it begins to thaw and then refreezes, causing another health hazard for my family.

The constant fluctuating temperatures inside of my fridge and freezer, the gas leaking out, and having to constantly defrost the fridge in order to have my ice maker work for a few days are all causing health hazards for my family, and Samsung refuses to do anything about the problem.
justification: The chemical smell and potential poisoning risk to the family, especially children, indicates a health hazard that could lead to injury.

incident_description: I went to use an Amazon Basics Multi-Speed Immersion Hand Blender. When it was plugged in I pressed the on button to trigger the protected propeller blade inside the cup to spin in order to check its speed before inserting it into a cup with liquid. As soon as I pressed the on button, not only did the propeller blade inside the silver cup begin to spin, but the whole bottom half of the machine vibrated at such a high frequency that my left hand that was next to it on the counter got immediately lacerated to shreds by the silver (seemingly protective) cup that turned out to also be as razor sharp as the protected blade inside. I bled profusely and was rushed to the ER where I received 8 stitches, hand x-rays, and an entire forearm splint. I was incredibly lucky that it was just the inside of my hand rather than right below on my wrist where it could have been fatal. I'm deeply concerned for the safety of others with this product, I'm incredibly traumatized from it.

In less than a minute the bottom of the mug exploded and began burning  with large flames and a very dense, acrid, black, fine-particled smoke. Opened microwave door and new oxygen caused flames to increase. Closed door and flames died down for lack of oxygen and then went out. Removed charged remains and set outdoors to continue smoldering and then go out. Opened all windows to remove dense smoke going throughout the house. In all of the materials received from purchase there was no mention of the extreme danger of placing the cup in the microwave--just one brief statement in small print, "Do not microwave." My concern is that there was no mention of the extreme danger of placing the cup in the microwave and the explosion and flames that would result. Were such a statement of danger prominent in the written materials and also on the cup, I would have been adequately forewarned of the danger and not inadvertently placed the cup in the microwave. The microwave was also destroyed and is being replaced.
justification: The incident involved an explosion and flames but no injury, and the likelihood is unlikely as it requires specific misuse of the product.

incident_description:
I own the samsung over oven range microwave (model#me21m706BAG) and it started acting funny suddenly and constantly beeping and the display screen saying press start to continue or stop. All through the day and middle of the night. One day I put my cup of coffee in the microwave for 1.00 (1minute) and take a call in my office. I realize after that I forgot my coffee, but when I walked back I saw the microwave still running and counting down from 45 minutes! I have no idea what happened! The next day the beeping continues and the display says press start or stop to clear I decided to press start for the first time and it started counting down from 7 seconds. I realized that this was related to the coffee incident and that this microwave now has a say itself on the time settings- it set my 1 minute entry and added a 7 to it so it must have attempted to run for 71 minutes! When I go to Samsungs website to get help and google if this has happened to any other people I saw that this is such a common defect that all reviewers have in common. Samsung hasn't placed a recall on this, but it is legitimately dangerous and entirely not functioning how a microwave is intended to. The beeping is annoying, but the software glitch causing the microwave to input its own time setting. When a microwave gains some control over it's settings you know there is a serious glitch. Constantly attempting to start itself and causing modifications to the time the consumer enters actually scares me. It is not like the glitch is only related to the number 7 here, it's a glitch in the keypad or software that operates the settings-as in the start button next to the number buttons! I don't know what else will happen since the faulty functionality has increased in frequency since it tried to melt my coffee cup (microwave safe has a limit and thankfully it wasn't food that could have actually caught on fire after 30+ minutes with the intent 71 total minutes). Some reviewers have said that theirs has had their doors replaced or the entire unit has been replaced, but it developed the same defect very soon after. This seems to be a very well known product defect to samsung, and obviously not something a consumer should expect from a microwave. I do not believe warranties are meant to capture a known defect to software like this, so the continued sales of it is placing an added financial burden and threat to safety on the consumers who apparently have no options to require Samsungs faulty product be recalled and replaced with non faulty units. Honestly just imagine not allowing your 7 and 9 year old to use a microwave because you fear that a faulty setting could impact the entered time and setting in such a way that could be dangerous. A casual popcorn setting could lead to harm of persons and property. I have never complained about a microwave or submitted a report about a dangerous product- and microwaves are so basic. But this entirely reminds me of the samsung phones that blew up and caught fire all over, this software however is inside a much larger and potentially dangerous piece of equipment. 

I realize that if I was standing  in front of the microwave after entering 1.00 start I could have noticed the faulty setting sooner, but realistically how often would a normal consumer do that? I imagine this could happen a lot, just as simply and randomly it had to me. I know a lot of kids who are perfectly old enough to operate a microwave, and I wonder what would have happened if they put a hot pocket in for 1 minute and continued their tv or game only to have their microwave burn the house down. I am genuinely confused why this has not already been recalled for clear defective software and the only thing I can think is that so far no one, or not enough someone's have died. That is good, but not what I personally feel is the bar for considering this safe. And because it is so well know to Samsung I am upset that I have to report this simply because their bar for what constitutes unsafe is when their phones explode. I was not harmed in this other than burning my hand trying to get the boiling sludge cup out of the microwave and into the sink, but I am a Chef so not a big deal personally. But I know fats and sugars or a paper plate/paper towel etc would not have responded the same as a cup of black coffee. I lucked out, and  I am appropriately aware and concerned.

Oh by the way the glitch does stack on top of itself. it beeps once and it's apparently setting it's time for 7 seconds, but if I do not clear it and it beeps again it is then set for 77 seconds....and so on. So just now while typing this I had to go clear it and when I decided out of curiosity how many beeps just occurred by pressing start I see it set itself for 77.77minutes....by itself. 

I'm having to explain to friends that visit to be careful and not use it because If my microwave hasn't gained consciousness and decided to try and kill me recently, than it seems like Samsung seems to be. lol. (trying to laugh off the $450 fire hazard in the making is the best I can do other than this report). 

Some reviewers have mentioned that the microwave turned on automatically as well, and I believe that has happened to mine as well. I'm just not in the room when it happened. I half thought we had a ghost or something, but this microwave has a mind of it's own and electromagnetic radiation designed to create thermal energy...I would have honestly preferred a ghost!
justification: The microwave's software glitch poses a risk of injury or property damage due to uncontrolled operation, as evidenced by the coffee incident and potential for fire hazards.

incident_description:
The product I am reporting is the E.G.O. Gas Reigniter, Part Number 83.22000.008 - commonly sold as part number PA020041 for a Viking stove.  This product was originally manufactured by Tytronics and is often still referred to as the Tytronics 0+4 spark module, but I Tytronics was sold to EGO back in 2012. 

This product is the module which produces the spark necessary to ignite a flame for a gas stove, in my case it is the listed replacement part for my Viking 6-burner stove.

My original module died in mid 2020 - the stove is from 1995 so I attribute this to regular end-of-life for the part.  A replacement was ordered from an online appliance retailer and installed following all instruction, direction, and standard practice.  

The module does not perform like the original.  It sparks multiple times to ignite (the original one gave one spark, MAYBE two, to ignite). It sparks continuously at lower flame settings (the original one was stable at all flame ranges). And worst of all - if the electrode is grounded to the burner, even with the gas off, the module sparks - I found this out while wiping the stove down with a wet rag, which was enough to give me an unpleasant shock (this NEVER happened with the older module).

I contacted the part website, they sent me a replacement, I installed it - same issue. They sent me a 2nd replacement - same issue. I contacted Viking, they suggested I swap the original igniter that is still on the 2 burner side, over to the 4 burner side. I checked each and every wire, ensured good ground to the module, ensured each gas control knob was properly working (Open circuit when off, zero resistance to ground when the gas is on) - I ensured all the wires were correctly oriented and I didn't have cross-zone issues. The older module works perfectly on the 4 burner side, and the new module works exactly as described above on the 2-burner side. In short - it's not an issue with my stove or the wiring, it's an issue with the module.  I contacted E.G.O. and they refuse to help me citing that "legally we cannot work with the end user".

To be specific - my concern is with the EGO Spark Module and the hazard is that it will shock users despite being properly installed.  EGO's unwillingness to discuss or address this issue, despite it being present in multiple units, is alarming.  The potential for others to get injured, or for a fire to accidentally start and cause significant damage, exists with this product.
justification: The incident describes an unpleasant shock from the module, indicating an injury (severity 3). The issue is present in multiple units, making occurrence likely (4).

incident_description:
LG's 2 year old dishwasher nearly burned my house down then they quietly closed 6 cases I opened with 6 representatives to discuss the matter along with the damage their dangerous equipment caused.  On the 6th attempt, I asked the representative if it was normal for the previous 5 cases to automatically be closed without any communications, she confirmed it was very odd and she never saw that happen before (all calls were recorded).  Additionally, both racks rusted through after 2 years of use.  LG agreed to send replacement racks since it was under warranty but they were never delivered.  The LG dishwasher also created water damage under the counter, which resulted in a 6' crack under the counter.

The root cause was the result of extremely poor engineering by LG.  1) Poorly designed seal which didn't use common design engineering knowledge 2) an extremely poorly designed latch design, which places a hole in the latch an inch away from the poorly designed seal.  The major safety hazard here is that the hole in the latch provides a direct path to the electrical switches in the door latch assembly.  These issues are further discussed below.

I originally provided LG with a video showing how their dishwasher shorted and burned at the LG dishwasher door latch switch.  I discovered the melted door latch assembly and exposed shorted wires because the dishwasher smelled like it was burning.  They clearly have design and quality issues.  The risk is too high to ever consider an LG appliance again.  I also have a 6 month old LG refrigerator and the compressor is occasionally making loud noises...  more quality issues with another LG appliance.  I also had the [REDACTED] for two years.  It was a horrible [REDACTED].  [REDACTED]provided infrequent updates.  So glad I returned to [REDACTED]...  anyways...

Here is the video showing the charred and melted door latch after it nearly burned my house down.  I also included a second video to diagnose the issue, since there was no longer power to the unit.

[REDACTED]

I bought their control board (potted PCBA) for about $200 and a door latch assembly with the correct switches.  After installing the new board and latch assembly, I learned that the dishwasher seal suffered from excessive compression set due to a poor mechanical design by LG.  Compression set is when the rubber remains compressed and doesn't return to it's original shape.  This typically occurs when rubber is compressed at more than 50%.  The problem can be easily avoided by limiting seal compression to a maximum of 50%.  This is basic design engineering knowledge but apparently, LG failed with that very trivial design requirement.

In addition to a poorly designed seal, it turns out that my house almost burned down because of a really, really bad LG latch design where the latch opening created direct access to the electrical switches.  This is a major safety hazard because the seal preventing water from leaking is about an inch away from the switches; this creates a direct path from the seal to the switches.  Water was leaking through the top of the seal and directly through the latch assembly and into the switches.  The distance from the seal to the switches is about 1 inch so if it leaks, it can cause a fire.  The same issue was going to happen again if I continued using the dishwasher.  At this point, it's clear there is a safety hazard.  I will likely start connecting with class action law firms to take further action, since LG continues to quietly close all cases I opened to discuss the matter.

It is incredibly alarming that LG would learn of this information and choose to quietly silent my cases.  It seems like LG doesn't care about the safety of their customers since they have not responded to my very troubling concerns.

I'm sure this will elicit a canned response from LG and a request to settle it privately.  However, it is troubling that they wouldn't want to make this issue well-known and have a safety recall.  My house almost burned down and they quietly closed 6 cases I opened.  LG's behavior is beyond unethical.  It's also beyond negligent.  It seems like it approaches criminal.  I can only imagine what other safety hazards they are covering up.

There are so many horrible reviews and stories from so many people about LG.  I had a bad experience with them last year, which led to me buying another refrigerator after less than 2 years of having the new refrigerator... which also has problems.  At this point, maybe I should notify the major retailers of the need to have a safety recall.  They may not care about their customers, but they will care about the cost and brand issues associated with a major safety recall... especially when they tried covering it up.
justification: The incident involved a near fire and property damage but no injury or death, warranting severity level 2. The likelihood is high (4) due to documented design flaws and multiple similar complaints.

I pulled my stove out and noticed a burnt area on my wall.  When I looked at the back of the stove, I noticed a small hole in the aluminum cover plate that covers the electrical connections, along with the tip of a screw sticking through the hole.  I removed the cover and found it too had burn marks on it. I then noticed that the terminal block had melted (it's made mostly of plastic), allowing both the hot and neutral terminals to move forward, with the hot terminal touching the aluminum cover plate.  Although there was short circuit on the 50 amp 240 circuit as a result of the hot terminal coming into contact with the cover plate, the 50 amp circuit breaker did not trip.  I became concerned when the stove arced even when it was turned off by my simply bumping into it.   I am immediately replacing this stove with a new one since this one is clearly a safety hazard.  I was very lucky that it didn't catch my house on fire or electrocute me when I bumped against the stove. I have photographs of the damage if you need it.

incident_description:
Product: Cuisinart 2-Slice Classic Metal Toaster
Model: GB-CPT160P1ESP 15CE015765
Purchased online from KohlÃÂs, received the product on 11/24/2020

Timeline:
11/24/2020 ÃÂ Received the product via UPS Shipment
11/27/2020 ÃÂ Tested the product before giving it to adult family member. Testing the toaster raised safety and hazard issues.
11/27/2020 ÃÂ Created and posted a 1-star review on KohlÃÂs website
11/30/2020 ÃÂ Called KohlÃÂs customer service # to report issues, was given a full refund, safety issues were raised to KohlÃÂs customer service manager.
11/30/2020 ÃÂ Called Cuisinart Customer Service # to report issues. The customer service representative told me that someone from corporate would call me within 48 to 72 hours. As of 12/4/2020, No one from the Cuisinart Brand management or Conair management has contacted me to discuss the productÃÂs safety issues.

Safety Issues:
1)	Product seems to be drawing too much electrical current to not work on a GFI receptacle.
2)	Product isn't designed or insulated to keep the sides cool/warm to the touch, like predecessor older models
3)	Product can cause significant burns to your skin or possibly cause a fire to occur.

I've recently purchased this new 2-Slice Classic Brushed Stainless metal toaster (model CPT-160) for my son's college apartment. Before giving it to my son, I plugged it into my kitchen GFI receptacle to test it..... the same outlet that my current older 4-slice Cuisinart toaster is plugged into. With the toasting setting on 3, this new toaster wouldn't work on a GFI receptacle, the toaster levers wouldn't stay down, and the toaster would not function. I tested the toaster on several GFI receptacles throughout the house and the toaster would not function. I then tested it on a non-GFI receptacle, and the levers engaged, and the toaster worked. I then noticed a horrible chemical odor emitting from the toaster as it was being used for the very first time. After the toasting cycle was completed, I picked up the toaster and moved it back to the kitchen counter. I then noticed how incredibly hot the toaster's outer metal shell was, and this was holding it from the bottom. After placing the toaster on the counter, I felt the bottom portion of the sides and they were too hot to keep my hands there. I then did a quick finger touch to the top portion of the sides and it was extremely hot.... like a hot skillet, and if I kept my finger there long enough, I would have gotten burns on my skin. Keep in mind that this was the sides of the toaster, not the top. With my current older 4-slice version of this Cuisinart Classic Style toaster, you can safely touch the sides of the toaster during and after the toasting cycle.... you can actually hold your hand pressed to the sides near the top without getting burned, as the older version, model CPT-180 only gets moderately warm to the touch.
It seems to me that this newly manufactured toaster, model CPT-160 is drawing too much electrical current to not work on a GFI receptacle and isn't designed or insulated to keep the sides cool/warm to the touch during the toasting cycle, and the outer stainless steel metal shell is noticeably thinner compared to my older 4-slice Classic Style Cuisinart toaster.
Over the past 20+ years, I've bought two Cuisinart 4-slice Classic Style metal toasters and was always happy with the quality of this Cuisinart toaster. The predecessor, older versions were well-made.
This new 2-slice Cuisinart Classic Style metal toaster, model CPT-160 can cause significant burns to your skin or possibly cause a fire to occur. This newly manufactured product should have failed many safety tests, in my opinion, and should be removed from the market immediately. I can only assume that Conair Corporate and Cuisinart Brand management has decided to cheapen their products now, use lessor quality of materials, cut corners in the engineering and safety processes to reduce costs, and produce more revenue.
justification: The toaster poses burn risks and potential fire hazards, but no actual injury or death was reported.

Also, machine does not show how clean the pipes are after the cleaning. So even if there is a fungus or dirt in the pipes, there is no way user would know.
- glass fiber is used beneath the hot plate which could get mixed with the rotis after wear and tear.
- no paid option from the Rotimatic in case of hardware issues. Other than warranty period there is no way to fix these issues.
- Basically any user who is using this machine for 4-5 months, is already eating breads (rotis) with fungus or dirt mixed.

What type of product(s) were being used?
Rotimatic - daily bread maker: https://rotimatic.com

Who was using the product(s)?
Probably at least a million users by now world wide. Not sure of their US sales count. In our home everyone ate the breads made by this machine for about 2 to 3 years.

How were the product(s) being used?
Daily, to make the bread.

Were there any injuries that happened or may have happened while using the product?
No injuries.

How did any injuries occur?
See my comment above on the hygenic part.
justification: The incident involves a malfunctioning and unhygienic food-making machine with no reported injuries, but potential health risks due to fungus and dirt contamination.

incident_description: . I purchased a Ninja Foodi 64 oz blender [Model No HB152] and used it for ~6 months until the glass pitcher exploded in my face on 10/10/20. I was unfortunate to discover this when an averaged-sized ice cube was accelerated into the thick glass pitcher with so much force that it exploded. I was hit with glass in the chest, and glass shards & milkshake continued to fly all over the kitchen (the blades continued to spin until I unplugged it). I am so so thankful that I didn't lose my eyesight. A well-meaning customer service rep today told me that I was not eligible for a refund, & if I paid for shipping I could receive a replacement of the same model.

incident_description: purchased a Samsung refrigerator in 8/2016. In May of this year we started to notice the temperature in the freezer did not match what they were set for. This was not acceptable to me and I spoke with a supervisor and was able to get an appt. on May 20 with a different tech. On May 20, a new tech came and was able to replace the compressor and requested us to call in 24 hrs to see if the unit was cooling. The next day we called because the fridge did seem to be keeping things frozen. The unit worked fine until 7/25/20 when we noticed that the freezer was again not maintaining temps despite the setting on the unit. Items weren't at safe temperatures. I reported this to Samsung, that the same issue was reoccurring and they agreed to send out a tech who would have to deem the unit "unrepairable" before they could refund us for the defective fridge but the first appointment was 8/13/20. LG LCRT1513ST /00 Microwave oven (manuf. July 2013), 
SN: 307TAQP59356 (uncertain if 2nd character is zero or letter "o").

On first use of day (a.m.), heated 2 cups of water in [REDACTED] measuring cup on High setting in LG microwave oven (LG). After 1-2 minutes became aware of heavy smoke coming from LG. Smoke was toxic, electronic melting smell of light gray/tan color. Emissions set off both smoke detector and CO detector in next room (separate units, both installed since 2018). Opened door to stop LG operation. Retrieved fire extinguisher and shot retardant into oven chamber and stood back to assess. Oven chamber light and display panel still on.

Re-approached LG and felt very warm-to-hot temperature on top, right exterior casing (above and behind control panel). While reaching to unplug power cord, LG beeped and switched off oven light and display (normal timer operation of "ECO-On" feature). Unplugged LG power cord from wall and moved LG outside for safety.

Outside air conditions in our area on 12 September 2020 were "Unhealthy" due to regional fires and other climate conditions. However, the air quality inside our house due to the LG smoke was much worse than outside.

(https://www.epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data/air-quality-index-daily-values-report)
Geographic Area: San Mateo County (California), 
Date: 09/12/2020, 
Overall PM2.5 AQI Value: 173 ("Unhealthy")

Later removed the top cover from LG and found the large capacitor block under the magnetron had melted itself and nearby wires. There were also burn marks around it and above on the inside of the top cover. The internal fuse did not blow. The dedicated 20A circuit the LG was plugged into did not reset (new panel, breakers and 20A circuit installed/inspected 2016).

Have extensive photos of the damage with part/serial #s. We do not believe the fire extinguisher had any effect on the electrical fire/melting as there was no direct access to that area from the cooking chamber. The [REDACTED] glass was still full of water and the cooking chamber looked fine except for being covered in retardant powder.

Luckily the fire was contained inside the microwave's case and only slight singing can be seen on the countertop underneath. The greater damage was to our lungs and health.
justification: The incident involved toxic smoke and potential health impacts, but no direct injury or death was reported.

incident_description:
At a child's 12-month well exam, his weight velocity had increased exponentially with no known cause. He had started to gain velocity in his weight around 6 months of age. At that time, there was no concern, as babies frequently change their curve and then curve off again as they get more active (crawling, walking, etc.). When I saw him for the first time, at his 9-month visit, the weight gain increased in velocity again. He was an overall happy and healthy infant, with a couple of minor developmental delays (again small concerns), and I didnÃÂt see any major issues, so we just discussed proper nutrition for an infant and the division of responsibility, a common concept to assure there is no overfeeding, as well as mixing formula properly, etc. I expected his weight to curve off at our next visit. I told the parents if there were concerns before then, we could do another weight check, but they didn't come in sooner. He started working with a birth-to-3 program for the developmental delays in between the time I saw him at his 9mo and then at 12mo when he weighed in at 40 lbs. I ran a huge panel of labs to check for metabolic disorders, and the only abnormality was mildly elevated triglycerides (the lipid associated with consuming too much sugar). I was certain, at this point, the parents were either lying to me, and he was overfeeding (based on these results) or some piece of information was definitely missing. At the 12mo visit, they claimed he was taking 24oz of 20kcal formula and ~8oz purees per day (he wasnÃÂt very into solids yet and was set for a feeding evaluation with the birth-to-3 program about this soon). I scheduled a virtual visit with them and had dad take me into the kitchen and show me the preparation of the formula to assure they werenÃÂt making a mistake and giving him formula that is too highly caloric. As he was walking into the kitchen, he mentioned that for the past 6 months or so (the first time we noted his weight velocity increasing), they have been using the Baby Brezza. They originally bought it for night feeds, so they wouldnÃÂt have to mix formula at night, but it was so convenient, they started using it all the time. He showed it to me, and I did a quick google search and found a couple scattered reports of inaccurate formula to water ratios. I advised them to immediately stop using this device and to come back in 1 month for a weight check. For the first time since his 6mo well exam, his weight curved off to what is considered a normal curve showing that this was almost certainly the cause of his weight gain and very likely why he hasnÃÂt been interested in solids (he was too full to be interested). He has likely been receiving very highly caloric formula for >6mo. After further research, I found out there is a class-action lawsuit against the company for the opposite complaint of not enough formula to water causing failure to thrive in babies. This is an incredibly unsafe product if it is not able to be consistent with its water to formula powder ratio. Failure to thrive and excessive weight gain causing developmental delays (e.g. this child can't get from lying down to sitting at 12 months of age due to being too obese) are some of the less serious outcomes I could imagine. If a child has the wrong formula to water ratio, they can have kidney failure, receive too much potassium causing their hearts to stop, etc. I am incredibly fearful of this machine as a health care provider. 

For the estimated date below, I just went back about 6 months from when he came in for his 12mo visit, but I'm not sure when they bought the product.
justification: The incident involves excessive weight gain and developmental delays due to incorrect formula preparation, but no immediate injury or death occurred.
